accepted.reason: Observation-target alignment is good for hospitalization-rate via delayed_I, consistent with surveillance semantics. SEIRS is parsimonious for a single season yet allows waning if needed, without introducing an explicit H compartment that is likely weakly identifiable with only 31 training weeks. No fractional memory, reducing overfitting risk.

Same strengths as proposal 0 (aligned delayed_I mapping; avoids explicit H identifiability issues; no fractional memory). A 3-week lag is plausible for admissions in some settings, so it is reasonable to keep as an alternative timing hypothesis, though it risks phase shift if true lag is shorter/variable.

Very parsimonious and aligned (delayed_I to hospitalization-rate) with low identifiability risk. Useful as a baseline comparator to test whether adding waning immunity (SEIRS) is necessary within this short single-season window; no fractional memory.

rejected.reason: Although H maps directly to the target, adding an explicit hospitalization compartment increases state/parameter complexity and is flagged as weakly identifiable for short single-season series. With 31 training weeks, admission/duration parameters can trade off with transmission/ascertainment, risking unstable fits without clear observational leverage.

I+H observation map is poorly aligned to a hospitalization-rate target because it mixes infectious burden with hospitalized prevalence, creating attribution ambiguity (two latent sources for one signal). This increases identifiability risk beyond proposal 2 and can encourage overfitting peak height/width without clear mechanistic justification in the surveillance note.

suggested_edits.edit: Clarify that the 3-week delay is intended as a discrete alternative to the 2-week lag (not an additional degree of freedom), and note that within-season variable lag could be approximated by choosing between 2 vs 3 weeks rather than fitting both.

If kept for consideration, constrain/justify hospitalization timescale parameters (e.g., fix or tightly bound average length-of-stay / admission-to-discharge rate) to reduce weak identifiability in a 31-week single-season series; otherwise prefer delayed_I.

If retained, narrow the observation map to H only (or justify a fixed weighting between I and H rather than free mixing) to reduce non-identifiability from explaining one hospitalization-rate series with two correlated latent components.
State explicitly that SEIR is a baseline and may miss late-season tail/rebound if waning is present; keep delay fixed at 2 weeks to avoid adding flexibility that could mimic waning.
